newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila reserve requirement cut hailed by banks.
newsitem.headline: Manila reserve requirement cut hailed by banks.

text.p: The Philippine's central bank signalled an easing in monetary policy on Thursday, shaving the reserve requirement for banks by two percentage points.
Analysts said the drop in the rate to 13 percent from 15 percent, which will be implemented in two phases over 1997, will likely translate into lower short-term money market rates.
The easing in policy follows a slowdown in inflation growth and will be the first cut in the key bank reserve requirement rate since May 1995.
Philippine Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said the bank will cut the rate by one percentage point on January 3 and again by another point on July 4.
The easing would effectively release 13.4 billion pesos ($510 million) in funds into the market, Singson said.
"With the notable slowdown in the inflation rate in recent months, this is an appropriate time to further reduce the reserve requirement to levels comparable with Asian countries," he said.
Economists said the cut could drive the benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate down to a 10-11 percent range in 1997 from the latest 1996 average of 12.4 percent.
The current 91-day T-bill rate is 11.7 percent.
But the easing was unlikely adversely impact the peso, the analysts said, adding that the local currency should be buoyed by relatively strong confidence in the economy.
The government had helped improve sentiment on the economy by implementation a tax reform bill which should ensure a long-term budget surplus position, the economists said.

"The dollar inflows will compensate for the reduction in interest rate differential (versus the U.S. dollar)," said Manny Lim, vice president of ING Bank, referring inflows of U.S. dollars due to the positive investment environment.
"The impact of stable interest and inflation could see the peso trading at 26.20-26.50 (to the dollar) next year," he said.
The peso closed on Thursday at around 26.292.
"I see a two percent depreciation on average to about 26.70 percent," said Emma Pante, economist at the Far East Bank.
The Central Bank would have pursued a cut in reserve requirements earlier this year but was held back by a surge in inflation into double-digit growth due to a rice shortage.
Inflation has since decelerated to single-digit levels in June this year. The latest year-on-year inflation was 4.7 percent in October versus 11 percent in the year-ago month.

"Monetary authorities will ensure that domestic liquidity generated from lower required reserves is kept within limits of the monetary programme and consistent with the inflation target of 6.5 percent in 1997," Singson said.
Central Bank research director Diwa Gunigundo told Reuters the 13.4 billion pesos that will be freed will result in an additional 54.8 billion pesos ($2.087 billion) to total domestic liquidity.
"We are not concerned," he said, since the Central Bank was able to successfully control money supply.
Gunigundo said the cut in reserve requirements will result in lower lending rates next year. Short-term prime lending rates are currently at 14 to 15 percent.
